scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Archeological excavations in Lurish-inhabited areas—including Kozagaran, Tepe Giyan, Tepe Musiyan, CheghaMish, and Kul-e Farah—demonstrate that Lurish dance predates Aryan migrations into the Iranian plateau.
Pottery motifs depicting three dancing figures and bronze flags from Luristan dating to the first millennium BC provide physical evidence of ancient dance traditions.
Musicians and instruments depicted on petroglyphs in Kul-e Farah and CheghaMish further confirm the antiquity of dance across these regions.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dances are performed for life-cycle events, seasonal work, and ritual commemorations.
Čupi and scarf dances feature prominently at weddings and festive gatherings.
Čubâzi serves as a celebratory martial spectacle, often presented as a prelude to weddings.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Lurish dances include circular group styles (Čupi), scarf dances (Dasmâl-bâzi), and martial stick duels (Čubâzi).
In Čupi, dancers join hands or fingers shoulder-to-shoulder, guided by a lead dancer called the Sarčupi (or Čupikeš).
Watch for Sangin-Samâ step, Sepâ step, Čubâzi leap.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circular chain lead by a Sarčupi, moving counter-clockwise or in place; or paired central dueling space.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Lurish dance relies heavily on traditional wind and percussion instruments, such as the karnâ horn, drums, strike instruments, and fiddles (often referred to as tochmal music).
The drum and horn accompaniment regulates the progressive speed of Čupi dances, accelerating from the slow tempo of Sangin-Samâ into the rapid beat of Dopâ.
Listen for the karnâ, sorna, drum, fiddle.
The pulse is 4/4 or 2/4 at about 105 beats a minute.
A driving combination of resonant outdoor horn calls (karnâ), melodic fiddle lines, and heavy drum strikes that steadily build in speed to propel circle dancers.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright, shoulder-to-shoulder contact in circular lines with elbows bent.
Pinky fingers linked at shoulder height, or waving colorful scarves held in both hands.
Controlled torso following directional step movements.

scenes.title: Count and rhythm
narration: Count: 1-2-3-4 then 5-6-7-8 (eight counts, two bars). The meter is 4/4 or 2/4.
Rhythm pattern: Slow steady pulse accelerating into rapid driving drum strikes..
Clap it first, then step it in place.

Metronome at 73 bpm

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Cross the right foot over the left foot.
Step 2: Take two steps forward.
Footwork from the sources: Right foot crosses left, two steps forward, left toe touch to side, stepping forward right-left-right with knee flexion.
Drill: Practice right-across-left cross steps in place.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Touch the tip of the left toe to the ground.
Step 4: Bring the left foot beside the right foot.
Drill: Add two steps forward and the left toe touch.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Hold arms bent at elbow with pinky finger engagement.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid breaking the locked hand-holding line in Čupi; in Čubâzi, strikes must never target above the knee.

visual_brief.setting_notes: Dances are performed for life-cycle events, seasonal work, and ritual commemorations. Čupi and scarf dances feature prominently at weddings and festive gatherings. Čubâzi serves as a celebratory martial spectacle, often presented as a prelude to weddings. Other specialized forms include harvesting ceremony dances, PaPoshtePa dances, Suwaruna, and solemn mourning dances such as Chamariuna performed for deceased loved ones among Feylis and Southern Lur tribes.
